screens.title: Troubleshooting Routing Protocol Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Routing protocols are the core organizers of enterprise traffic. In this lesson you will learn a practical, methodical approach to diagnosing OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP problems so you can restore stable routing without creating additional faults. We begin by building a checklist: verify interface and IP connectivity, confirm matching protocol parameters, inspect neighbor states, examine route tables and protocol databases, and use targeted debug commands under controlled conditions. For example, when OSPF adjacency fails, checking hello and dead timers or network type mismatches often reveals the cause faster than broad resets. In EIGRP, a stuck-in-active condition usually means a neighbor didn't respond to a query; the appropriate commands show which routes remain unresolved. In BGP, a session stuck in Active most commonly points to TCP connectivity issues on port 179 or an AS misconfiguration. A common misconception is that running a global reset will fix every issue; in production that can cause major outages. Instead, learn to gather the right show outputs, scope your debug filters, and plan a rollback. By the end of this module you will have clear diagnostic sequences and command pairs for each protocol and a safety-first mindset for making changes in live networks. What will you check first when a routing protocol goes silent?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Troubleshooting Routing Protocol Issues
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Troubleshooting Routing Protocol Issues

Learn repeatable diagnostic sequences for OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP, and how to use show and debug safely.

Orientation: This chapter focuses on diagnosing adjacency and route exchange failures, recognizing protocol-specific failure modes, and applying safe fixes. Expect command patterns, diagnostic outputs, and practical remediation steps rather than full configuration tutorials.

In this lesson

Stepwise debugging for OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP using show and debug tools with safety notes.

Why it matters

Routing faults can create outages. Precise diagnosis reduces downtime and avoids cascading problems.

Explore Key Topics
OSPF Adjacency

Timers, network types, authentication, and LSA visibility.

EIGRP Neighbors

Neighbor formation, SIA diagnostics, and summarization risks.

BGP Peering

Peer states, TCP connectivity, route advertisement, and attributes.

Visual Concept
Terminal-first Diagnostic Strip
show ip interface brief
show ip ospf interface Gig0/0
show ip eigrp neighbors
show ip bgp summary
Quick Tip
Start with interface and reachability checks before running heavy debug. Scoped debug saves CPU and reduces noise.

You will learn to identify and resolve OSPF adjacency and area misconfiguration problems, including hello/dead timer and network type mismatches, and to verify LSA propagation so that routes appear where they should. You will gain techniques to find EIGRP neighbor formation faults, interpret a Stuck-In-Active condition, and validate summarization and passive interface mistakes using the topology and neighbor commands. You will also acquire a practical workflow for BGP: verify TCP connectivity, check neighbor states, analyze received and advertised routes, and inspect BGP attributes that influence path selection. Throughout, you will practice using targeted show and debug commands safely, and understand common pitfalls like ACLs blocking updates, misapplied route-maps, and careless redistribution. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a lab or production-like environment. screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.narratorSegment: These additional objectives focus on preventing and validating fixes. You will learn to interpret protocol databases: OSPF LSAs, EIGRP topology entries, and the BGP RIB, so you can tell whether a route is missing because it was never advertised, filtered, or suppressed by policy. You will learn to read neighbor state indications and map them to causes — for example, OSPF stuck in Exchange often signals network type or MTU mismatch, while BGP stuck in Connect/Active points to TCP issues. You will also practice crafting and validating route-maps, prefix-lists, and redistribution rules so the routes you expect to flow between protocols do so in a controlled, tagged way. A common misconception is that redistribution alone is sufficient; in practice you must also control attributes and tags to prevent loops. These competencies reduce trial-and-error changes and give you confidence in live operations. Which protocol's database would you inspect first on a router that is missing a known network?

screens.title: OSPF adjacency formation
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF adjacency formation is the process by which two routers recognize each other as neighbors and exchange link-state information. Begin troubleshooting by verifying basic IP connectivity and that the physical and logical interfaces are up. Then confirm critical OSPF parameters: area ID, hello and dead timers, network type, and authentication configuration. For example, a common failure occurs when one side is configured as point-to-point and the other as broadcast; even with IP reachability, hellos may be discarded and adjacency will not form. To investigate, run show ip interface brief and show ip ospf interface on both routers to compare timers and types. Use debug ip ospf hello to observe hello packets and debug ip ospf adjacency to watch the adjacency state machine. A useful misconception check: OSPF process IDs do not need to match across routers for adjacency, so differing process numbers alone are rarely the cause. Also check ACLs that might drop multicast hellos. A concrete example: if Router A shows hello timer 10 seconds and Router B is set to 1 second, the mismatch prevents adjacency; aligning timers resolves it. Key takeaway: follow a small ordered checklist—connectivity, matching timers/types, authentication, then controlled debug—to reduce wasted changes. What verification would you run after aligning a mismatched timer to ensure the adjacency formed?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › OSPF adjacency formation
Definition

OSPF adjacency is when two routers form neighbor states and exchange LSAs to build a shared link-state database.

Common checks
  • Interface state and IP reachability (show ip interface brief).
  • OSPF area and network type (show ip ospf interface).
  • Hello/dead timer alignment and authentication settings.
  • ACLs or multicast blocking that drop 224.0.0.5 packets.
Concrete example
RouterA# show ip ospf interface Gig0/0
  Hello 10, Dead 40, Network Type BROADCAST
RouterB# show ip ospf interface Gig0/0
  Hello 1, Dead 4, Network Type BROADCAST

Mismatch: adjust RouterB hello to 10 to match RouterA.
Debug and verification

Use focused debug commands and verify LSA exchange after adjacency forms.

Scoped debug

debug ip ospf hello — watch hellos; debug ip ospf adjacency — track state transitions. Use filters and limit to maintenance windows on production routers.

Key Takeaway

Small parameter mismatches are the most common root cause. Fix parameters, verify LSA presence with show ip ospf database, then confirm route visibility.

screens.title: Diagnosing OSPF route advertisement failures
screens.narratorSegment: When an expected OSPF-learned route is missing from a router's routing table, follow a clear process: verify the local route source, check LSA presence across routers, confirm area boundaries and redistribution, and inspect filters. Start with show ip route ospf on the receiving router. If the route is missing, run show ip ospf database on all routers in the area to determine whether the LSA for that prefix exists. If LSAs are absent, consider area misconfiguration or redistribution omissions. For example, if an external route should be redistributed into OSPF but was advertised from a device in another routing domain, ensure redistribution statements include subnets and proper metrics. A common mistake is assuming that a route learned by the local routing table will automatically be redistributed; redistribution requires explicit commands and often the subnets keyword. If LSAs are present but the route is not installed, examine prefix lengths, route preference, and whether route filtering via distribute-lists or area virtual links is suppressing it. Use debug ip ospf lsa to observe LSA events during your test change in a lab. Conclude by confirming that show ip route ospf lists the prefix and that downstream routers see the same LSA. The key takeaway: systematically move from route table to LSDB to configuration and then to scoped debug to pinpoint where advertisement stops.

keyIdea.text: Trace from the routing table back into the OSPF LSDB and redistribution rules to find where advertisement stops.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Diagnosing OSPF route advertisement failures
Step-by-step
  1. show ip route ospf — confirm missing prefix.
  2. show ip ospf database — verify LSA exists in the area on all routers.
  3. Check redistribution and subnets keyword if route originated elsewhere.
  4. Inspect filters: distribute-lists, route-maps, area policies.
  5. Use debug ip ospf lsa with filters in a lab to watch LSA creation and flooding.
Example CLI snippets
show ip route ospf
show ip ospf database | include 10.10.0.0
show ip protocols
show run | section router ospf
debug ip ospf lsa
Takeaway

Work backwards from route absence to LSDB and configuration; redistribution and filtering are frequent causes.

screens.title: EIGRP neighbor formation fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP neighbors form adjacencies when several conditions align: matching autonomous system number, direct IP reachability, compatible K-values if authentication is applied, and that interfaces are not configured as passive. When you see an expected neighbor missing, start with show ip eigrp neighbors to see current adjacencies and show ip interface brief to validate reachability. If neighbors exist but routes are missing, inspect show ip eigrp topology to determine if entries are learning or flagged Active. Authentication mismatches are common, so confirm key-chain and key-id settings on both sides. Another common configuration error is an interface set to passive, which prevents forming a neighbor on that interface. Use show ip eigrp interfaces detail to confirm which interfaces are participating. A practical example: Router R2 shows a neighbor to R3 but has no topology entries for R3 networks; inspecting route-maps or distribute-lists applied to EIGRP often reveals filtering that blocks advertisement. Misconception check: unlike OSPF, EIGRP does not rely on area IDs, so area mismatches are not a factor — focus instead on AS and interface-level settings. Final verification: after correcting a passive-interface or auth mismatch, watch show ip eigrp neighbors and confirm routes appear in show ip route eigrp. How would you confirm a key-chain mismatch without changing live keys?

keyIdea.text: Confirm AS, IP reachability, no passive interfaces, and authentication key alignment before deeper topology checks.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › EIGRP neighbor formation fundamentals
What to check first
  • show ip eigrp neighbors — check adjacency table and uptime.
  • show ip interface brief — confirm the interfaces are up and IPs present.
  • show ip eigrp interfaces detail — verify participation and no passive flags.
  • Verify AS number and key-chains for authentication.
Example
R2# show ip eigrp neighbors
H   Address        Interface     Hold Uptime  SRTT   RTO  Q  Seq
0   10.0.0.3       Gi0/1         12  00:05:12  50   100  0  3
Misconceptions & tips

EIGRP does not use area IDs; beginners often look for OSPF-like area misconfigurations when AS or passive-interface is the real issue. Also avoid global clears; reset only affected neighborships after confirming cause.

Key Takeaway

Focus on AS, reachability, authentication, and passive-interface flags first. Then inspect topology for SIA symptoms if routes are missing.

screens.title: EIGRP Stuck-In-Active (SIA) diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: Stuck-In-Active (SIA) is an EIGRP condition where a router issues a query for a route but does not receive replies within the active timer, leaving the route waiting and potentially removed from the routing table. This differs from normal route recalculation, which completes when replies arrive quickly. To diagnose SIA, start with show ip eigrp topology active to list routes currently waiting for replies, and use debug eigrp packets query to observe outgoing queries and any replies. Common root causes include an unreachable neighbor, an overloaded neighbor that cannot respond promptly, or filtering that blocks the query or reply. For example, if R2 queries R3 for a route and R3 has an ACL blocking EIGRP packets, the reply never arrives and R2 will mark the route Active. A typical misconception is that simply increasing timers fixes SIA; while longer timeouts may hide underlying reachability or filtering faults, they do not correct the root cause. The proper remediation is to restore reachability, correct filtering, or adjust topology so queries have a clear next-hop path. After remediation, validate with show ip eigrp topology to confirm the route leaves Active and show ip route to confirm installation. Final check: confirm neighbors are stable and that query rates are reasonable to avoid repeated SIA events.

keyIdea.text: Use topology active and query debug to separate SIA caused by reachability/filtering from benign recalculation due to normal topology changes.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › EIGRP Stuck-In-Active (SIA) diagnosis
Symptoms
  • Routes in topology stuck in Active state.
  • Repeated queries with no replies recorded.
  • Potential route removal from routing table after timeout.
Commands
show ip eigrp topology active
debug eigrp packets query
show ip eigrp neighbors
Example scenario

R2 queries for 192.168.1.0. R3 receives query but has an ACL configured that drops EIGRP packets from R2. No reply is sent; R2 lists the route as Active and may remove it after the timer expires.

Common mistake

Raising timers without fixing filtering or reachability masks the issue and allows intermittent failures to persist undetected.

Check

After fixes, confirm show ip eigrp topology no longer shows Active entries and that routes are present in show ip route.

screens.title: Using show and debug safely
screens.narratorSegment: Debug commands are powerful but can overload a router if used broadly. A safe workflow: reproduce the symptom in a controlled window, run show commands to gather state, enable debug with filters or on a single neighbor, capture output, then disable debug immediately. Use show ip interface brief, show ip protocols, show ip route, and protocol-specific database commands first. For OSPF, prefer debug ip ospf hello or debug ip ospf adjacency rather than global LSA debug. For EIGRP, debug eigrp packets hello or debug eigrp packets query scoped to the interface in question. For BGP, debug ip bgp events is useful but run it with tight logging because BGP can generate frequent events. Example sequence for an OSPF adjacency problem: 1) show ip interface brief; 2) show ip ospf interface Gig0/0; 3) debug ip ospf hello on the two routers for a short period; 4) capture the hello mismatch and stop debug. A common misconception is that debug must run until the problem disappears; instead, capture a short window of output sufficient to diagnose and then stop. Always have a rollback or an alternate access path in case a debug command spikes C P U. Final check: after stopping debug, confirm C P U and adjacency state are normal with show processes and show ip ospf neighbor. Who should you notify before running debug on a production router?

keyIdea.text: Gather state with show commands, run scoped debug briefly with filters, capture output, then stop debug and verify CPU and protocol state.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Using show and debug safely

Safe command pattern

  1. Collect state with show commands to narrow the scope.
  2. Plan a short debug window and notify stakeholders.
  3. Run scoped debug or interface-specific debug and capture output.
  4. Stop debug immediately and verify CPU and protocol health.
Example sequence
show ip interface brief
show ip ospf interface Gig0/0
debug ip ospf hello (short duration)
no debug all
show ip ospf neighbor
Risk controls
  • Use maintenance windows when possible.
  • Limit debug to specific interface or neighbor.
  • Monitor CPU and have console access ready.
Final check

After debug, confirm normal CPU and stable neighbor states before declaring the issue resolved.

screens.title: BGP neighbor states and TCP reliance
screens.narratorSegment: BGP peers progress through a sequence of TCP and protocol states before exchanging routes. The key states are Connect and Active, which indicate TCP negotiation; OpenSent when a TCP session has established and the BGP OPEN was sent; and Established when routes can be exchanged. If a neighbor stays in Active or Connect, it usually points to TCP connectivity problems such as an ACL blocking port 179, incorrect neighbor IP, or no TCP reachability to the peer. Use show ip bgp summary to see state and use telnet neighbor-ip 179 from the router to test TCP connectivity. For example, if R1 shows the session as Active and telnet 10.0.0.4 179 from R1 fails, an intermediate device is likely blocking TCP 179. A misconception is to blame BGP configuration first; often the underlying TCP path is the issue. For deeper insight, debug ip bgp events shows state transitions but should be used cautiously. After restoring TCP connectivity, confirm peer state reaches Established and inspect show ip bgp neighbors neighbor-ip advertised-routes to validate what was sent. The final verification is to ensure expected prefixes appear in show ip bgp and that path attributes match intended policy. What immediate test would you run from the router to verify TCP reachability to a BGP peer?

keyIdea.text: If a BGP session is stuck in Active/Connect, verify TCP port 179 connectivity first, then inspect BGP config and filters.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › BGP neighbor states and TCP reliance
State meanings
Connect / Active

TCP has not completed; often indicates network or ACL issues blocking port 179.

OpenSent

BGP OPEN message was sent; waiting for OPEN from peer.

Established

Peers exchange updates; check advertised and received routes and attributes.

Example command
show ip bgp summary

screens.title: BGP route advertisement and filtering
screens.narratorSegment: When a prefix is expected in the BGP table but does not appear, the cause may be a missing network command, an incorrect redistribute statement, or filtering via route-maps, prefix-lists, or access-lists. Start with show ip bgp [network] to learn whether the route is known to BGP locally; if it is not present, check show ip bgp neighbors neighbor-ip advertised-routes to verify what you told the neighbor. If redistribution is used, confirm that the redistribute statement includes the proper protocols and the subnets keyword when necessary. For example, redistributing connected networks into BGP often requires explicit prefix insertion; forgetting the subnets keyword can drop specific host or subnet routes. Route-maps can also modify attributes such as AS_PATH, Local Preference, or MED, causing the path selection process to prefer other routes; inspect show ip bgp [network] to see attribute values. A common misconception is that a prefix absent from the BGP table is always filtered by an inbound policy; often the route was never injected into BGP on the origin router. After changes, validate with show ip bgp summary and show ip bgp neighbors to confirm routes are advertised and received. The takeaway: check origin configuration first, then inspect policies and attribute effects to understand why a route was not accepted or selected.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › BGP route advertisement and filtering

Root cause sequence

  • Confirm prefix exists locally (show ip route).
  • Check BGP origin and presence in RIB (show ip bgp [network]).
  • Inspect redistribute statements and subnets keyword.
  • Evaluate route-maps / prefix-lists / ACLs applied in or out of BGP neighbors.
CLI example
show ip bgp 203.0.113.0

show run | section router bgp
show ip prefix-list
Misconception

Assuming missing route means inbound filtering. Often the route was never originated into BGP or was removed by redistribution rules.

Takeaway

Work from the origin outward: local routing, redistribution, then neighbor advertisement and filtering.

screens.title: Route redistribution pitfalls and prevention
screens.narratorSegment: Redistribution exchanges routes between different routing protocols but can create loops or unexpected advertisements if not controlled. When redistributing, always tag redistributed routes and consider administrative distance adjustments to control preference. For example, when injecting EIGRP routes into OSPF, use route-maps to set a tag; on the receiving protocol, configure filters to prevent re-redistribution of the same tag back into the original protocol. A common pitfall is redistributing without subnets in protocols that require it, resulting in missing specific prefixes. Another is neglecting attribute control in BGP when redistributing into BGP; you should carefully set Local Preference, MED, or AS_PATH prepending via route-maps to influence selection. Begin troubleshooting redistribution by listing redistribution statements and route-maps with show run | section router and show route-map. Verify tagged routes with show ip route and show ip route to see origin. Misconception check: tagging and administrative distance are not alternatives; use both where appropriate—tags to prevent loops and administrative distance to prefer learned routes. After implementing safe redistribution, validate that the redistributed routes appear where expected and that no loops are present by tracing routes across protocols. The key takeaway: control what you redistribute and tag it so you can filter it later.

Best practices

  • Use route-maps to limit which prefixes are redistributed.

Example

When redistributing EIGRP into OSPF, tag EIGRP-injected routes with tag 200, then filter tag 200 on OSPF-to-EIGRP redistribution to avoid loops.

screens.title: Common mistakes across protocols
screens.narratorSegment: Across OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP, several recurring mistakes account for most trouble tickets. Authentication mismatches are frequently overlooked during upgrades or when keys are rotated; always compare key-chain and key-id settings. ACLs or firewall rules that block protocol-specific traffic—multicast hellos for OSPF, EIGRP packets, or TCP 179 for BGP—are another common culprit and should be checked early. Interface state errors such as shutdown or wrong IP addressing can mimic protocol failures; start troubleshooting with show ip interface brief. Timer mismatches are especially relevant for OSPF; mismatched hello/dead timers can prevent adjacency. EIGRP summarization and auto-summary can hide more-specific routes, while aggressive summarization causes black holes. Another frequent error is careless redistribution without tags or filters, leading to loops. To prevent these errors, keep a checklist: authentication, ACLs, interface up, timers/types, and summarization settings. A misconception to avoid: changing process IDs will fix adjacency; it usually will not. When you see a symptom, run a targeted set of show commands covering these categories before applying fixes. The takeaway: use a consistent checklist to avoid common human errors and rapidly narrow the root cause.

screens.title: Hands-on scenario: three-router troubleshooting lab
screens.narratorSegment: In the lab scenario you have R1, R2, and R3. R1 and R2 run OSPF Area 0, R2 and R3 use EIGRP AS 100, and R1 peers with an external BGP speaker R4. Three problems are presented: an OSPF adjacency failure between R1 and R2, EIGRP routes from R3 not appearing on R2, and R1's BGP session to R4 stuck in Active. For the OSPF adjacency, run show ip interface brief and show ip ospf interface GigX to compare hello/dead timers and network types; use debug ip ospf hello briefly to confirm parameter mismatch. For EIGRP, run show ip eigrp neighbors, show ip eigrp interfaces detail, and show ip protocols to find passive interfaces or distribute-lists; check show ip eigrp topology active if SIA is suspected. For BGP, run show ip bgp summary and telnet 10.0.0.4 179 from R1 to test TCP connectivity; inspect access-lists with show access-lists if telnet fails. A key operational concern: avoid broad clears like clear ip bgp * in production. Instead, after confirming fixes, reset only the affected neighbor or use soft-reconfiguration where available. After each fix, validate with the equivalent show commands to confirm the adjacency, neighbor, or session reached the desired state. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These core concepts are the anchors for troubleshooting routing protocols. First, OSPF adjacency depends on matching timers, network type, area ID, and authentication; mismatches there prevent LSA exchange. Second, EIGRP neighbor formation requires matching autonomous system number, interface reachability, and acceptable authentication; SIA indicates unanswered queries and usually points to reachability or filtering problems. Third, BGP peering relies on TCP connectivity on port 179; states like Active and Connect are often TCP path issues. Also remember route redistribution needs explicit configuration and tagging to avoid loops, and route-maps/prefix-lists are the tools that control what is advertised. Common operational mistakes include ACLs blocking protocol traffic, interface misconfiguration, timer mismatches, and aggressive summarization. Finally, always use a safe debug workflow: collect show outputs, run scoped debug briefly, stop debug, and validate. These ideas let you move quickly from symptom to root cause while minimizing production risk. Which core concept will you use first when you next see a missing route?

fullNarratorScript:
Routing protocols are the core organizers of enterprise traffic. In this lesson you will learn a practical, methodical approach to diagnosing OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP problems so you can restore stable routing without creating additional faults. We begin by building a checklist: verify interface and IP connectivity, confirm matching protocol parameters, inspect neighbor states, examine route tables and protocol databases, and use targeted debug commands under controlled conditions. For example, when OSPF adjacency fails, checking hello and dead timers or network type mismatches often reveals the cause faster than broad resets. In EIGRP, a stuck-in-active condition usually means a neighbor didn't respond to a query; the appropriate commands show which routes remain unresolved. In BGP, a session stuck in Active most commonly points to TCP connectivity issues on port 179 or an AS misconfiguration. A common misconception is that running a global reset will fix every issue; in production that can cause major outages. Instead, learn to gather the right show outputs, scope your debug filters, and plan a rollback. By the end of this module you will have clear diagnostic sequences and command pairs for each protocol and a safety-first mindset for making changes in live networks. What will you check first when a routing protocol goes silent?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to methodically diagnose and correct the most common routing protocol failures encountered in enterprise networks. You will learn to identify and resolve OSPF adjacency and area misconfiguration problems, including hello/dead timer and network type mismatches, and to verify LSA propagation so that routes appear where they should. You will gain techniques to find EIGRP neighbor formation faults, interpret a Stuck-In-Active condition, and validate summarization and passive interface mistakes using the topology and neighbor commands. You will also acquire a practical workflow for BGP: verify TCP connectivity, check neighbor states, analyze received and advertised routes, and inspect BGP attributes that influence path selection. Throughout, you will practice using targeted show and debug commands safely, and understand common pitfalls like ACLs blocking updates, misapplied route-maps, and careless redistribution. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a lab or production-like environment. These skills matter because precise diagnosis prevents cascading outages and ensures predictable route behavior under change. Which objective would you test first in your environment?

These additional objectives focus on preventing and validating fixes. You will learn to interpret protocol databases: OSPF LSAs, EIGRP topology entries, and the BGP RIB, so you can tell whether a route is missing because it was never advertised, filtered, or suppressed by policy. You will learn to read neighbor state indications and map them to causes — for example, OSPF stuck in Exchange often signals network type or MTU mismatch, while BGP stuck in Connect/Active points to TCP issues. You will also practice crafting and validating route-maps, prefix-lists, and redistribution rules so the routes you expect to flow between protocols do so in a controlled, tagged way. A common misconception is that redistribution alone is sufficient; in practice you must also control attributes and tags to prevent loops. Finally, you will practice a lab scenario that simulates adjacency failures across OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP and requires you to choose the right debug for each case. These competencies reduce trial-and-error changes and give you confidence in live operations. Which protocol's database would you inspect first on a router that is missing a known network?

OSPF adjacency formation is the process by which two routers recognize each other as neighbors and exchange link-state information. Begin troubleshooting by verifying basic IP connectivity and that the physical and logical interfaces are up. Then confirm critical OSPF parameters: area ID, hello and dead timers, network type, and authentication configuration. For example, a common failure occurs when one side is configured as point-to-point and the other as broadcast; even with IP reachability, hellos may be discarded and adjacency will not form. To investigate, run show ip interface brief and show ip ospf interface on both routers to compare timers and types. Use debug ip ospf hello to observe hello packets and debug ip ospf adjacency to watch the adjacency state machine. A useful misconception check: OSPF process IDs do not need to match across routers for adjacency, so differing process numbers alone are rarely the cause. Also check ACLs that might drop multicast hellos. A concrete example: if Router A shows hello timer 10 seconds and Router B is set to 1 second, the mismatch prevents adjacency; aligning timers resolves it. Key takeaway: follow a small ordered checklist—connectivity, matching timers/types, authentication, then controlled debug—to reduce wasted changes. What verification would you run after aligning a mismatched timer to ensure the adjacency formed?

When an expected OSPF-learned route is missing from a router's routing table, follow a clear process: verify the local route source, check LSA presence across routers, confirm area boundaries and redistribution, and inspect filters. Start with show ip route ospf on the receiving router. If the route is missing, run show ip ospf database on all routers in the area to determine whether the LSA for that prefix exists. If LSAs are absent, consider area misconfiguration or redistribution omissions. For example, if an external route should be redistributed into OSPF but was advertised from a device in another routing domain, ensure redistribution statements include subnets and proper metrics. A common mistake is assuming that a route learned by the local routing table will automatically be redistributed; redistribution requires explicit commands and often the subnets keyword. If LSAs are present but the route is not installed, examine prefix lengths, route preference, and whether route filtering via distribute-lists or area virtual links is suppressing it. Use debug ip ospf lsa to observe LSA events during your test change in a lab. Conclude by confirming that show ip route ospf lists the prefix and that downstream routers see the same LSA. The key takeaway: systematically move from route table to LSDB to configuration and then to scoped debug to pinpoint where advertisement stops.

EIGRP neighbors form adjacencies when several conditions align: matching autonomous system number, direct IP reachability, compatible K-values if authentication is applied, and that interfaces are not configured as passive. When you see an expected neighbor missing, start with show ip eigrp neighbors to see current adjacencies and show ip interface brief to validate reachability. If neighbors exist but routes are missing, inspect show ip eigrp topology to determine if entries are learning or flagged Active. Authentication mismatches are common, so confirm key-chain and key-id settings on both sides. Another common configuration error is an interface set to passive, which prevents forming a neighbor on that interface. Use show ip eigrp interfaces detail to confirm which interfaces are participating. A practical example: Router R2 shows a neighbor to R3 but has no topology entries for R3 networks; inspecting route-maps or distribute-lists applied to EIGRP often reveals filtering that blocks advertisement. Misconception check: unlike OSPF, EIGRP does not rely on area IDs, so area mismatches are not a factor — focus instead on AS and interface-level settings. Final verification: after correcting a passive-interface or auth mismatch, watch show ip eigrp neighbors and confirm routes appear in show ip route eigrp. How would you confirm a key-chain mismatch without changing live keys?

Stuck-In-Active (SIA) is an EIGRP condition where a router issues a query for a route but does not receive replies within the active timer, leaving the route waiting and potentially removed from the routing table. This differs from normal route recalculation, which completes when replies arrive quickly. To diagnose SIA, start with show ip eigrp topology active to list routes currently waiting for replies, and use debug eigrp packets query to observe outgoing queries and any replies. Common root causes include an unreachable neighbor, an overloaded neighbor that cannot respond promptly, or filtering that blocks the query or reply. For example, if R2 queries R3 for a route and R3 has an ACL blocking EIGRP packets, the reply never arrives and R2 will mark the route Active. A typical misconception is that simply increasing timers fixes SIA; while longer timeouts may hide underlying reachability or filtering faults, they do not correct the root cause. The proper remediation is to restore reachability, correct filtering, or adjust topology so queries have a clear next-hop path. After remediation, validate with show ip eigrp topology to confirm the route leaves Active and show ip route to confirm installation. Final check: confirm neighbors are stable and that query rates are reasonable to avoid repeated SIA events.

Debug commands are powerful but can overload a router if used broadly. A safe workflow: reproduce the symptom in a controlled window, run show commands to gather state, enable debug with filters or on a single neighbor, capture output, then disable debug immediately. Use show ip interface brief, show ip protocols, show ip route, and protocol-specific database commands first. For OSPF, prefer debug ip ospf hello or debug ip ospf adjacency rather than global LSA debug. For EIGRP, debug eigrp packets hello or debug eigrp packets query scoped to the interface in question. For BGP, debug ip bgp events is useful but run it with tight logging because BGP can generate frequent events. Example sequence for an OSPF adjacency problem: 1) show ip interface brief; 2) show ip ospf interface Gig0/0; 3) debug ip ospf hello on the two routers for a short period; 4) capture the hello mismatch and stop debug. A common misconception is that debug must run until the problem disappears; instead, capture a short window of output sufficient to diagnose and then stop. Always have a rollback or an alternate access path in case a debug command spikes C P U. Final check: after stopping debug, confirm C P U and adjacency state are normal with show processes and show ip ospf neighbor. Who should you notify before running debug on a production router?

BGP peers progress through a sequence of TCP and protocol states before exchanging routes. The key states are Connect and Active, which indicate TCP negotiation; OpenSent when a TCP session has established and the BGP OPEN was sent; and Established when routes can be exchanged. If a neighbor stays in Active or Connect, it usually points to TCP connectivity problems such as an ACL blocking port 179, incorrect neighbor IP, or no TCP reachability to the peer. Use show ip bgp summary to see state and use telnet neighbor-ip 179 from the router to test TCP connectivity. For example, if R1 shows the session as Active and telnet 10.0.0.4 179 from R1 fails, an intermediate device is likely blocking TCP 179. Interface state errors such as shutdown or wrong IP addressing can mimic protocol failures; start troubleshooting with show ip interface brief. Timer mismatches are especially relevant for OSPF; mismatched hello/dead timers can prevent adjacency. EIGRP summarization and auto-summary can hide more-specific routes, while aggressive summarization causes black holes. Another frequent error is careless redistribution without tags or filters, leading to loops. To prevent these errors, keep a checklist: authentication, ACLs, interface up, timers/types, and summarization settings. A misconception to avoid: changing process IDs will fix adjacency; it usually will not. When you see a symptom, run a targeted set of show commands covering these categories before applying fixes. The takeaway: use a consistent checklist to avoid common human errors and rapidly narrow the root cause.

These core concepts are the anchors for troubleshooting routing protocols. First, OSPF adjacency depends on matching timers, network type, area ID, and authentication; mismatches there prevent LSA exchange. Second, EIGRP neighbor formation requires matching autonomous system number, interface reachability, and acceptable authentication; SIA indicates unanswered queries and usually points to reachability or filtering problems. Third, BGP peering relies on TCP connectivity on port 179; states like Active and Connect are often TCP path issues. Also remember route redistribution needs explicit configuration and tagging to avoid loops, and route-maps/prefix-lists are the tools that control what is advertised. Common operational mistakes include ACLs blocking protocol traffic, interface misconfiguration, timer mismatches, and aggressive summarization.
